page.title: Top mistakes to avoid when deploying react apps to production
page.description: Common production issues in React apps, and how to avoid them before they reach users.

text.content: Deploying a React app can feel like the finish line of a project, but it’s really just the start of a new phase. Once real users are in the app, things get a lot less predictable. People are on slower networks, older devices, different browsers, and sometimes they click things in ways you absolutely did not expect.

rich_text.plain_text: Deploying a React app can feel like the finish line of a project, but it’s really just the start of a new phase. Once real users are in the app, things get a lot less predictable. People are on slower networks, older devices, different browsers, and sometimes they click things in ways you absolutely did not expect.

text.content: A good production deployment is not just about making sure the app works. It’s about making sure it works well, stays secure, loads quickly, and gives you enough visibility to fix issues when something goes wrong.

text.content: Here are some of the most common mistakes developers make when deploying React apps to production, plus a few practical ways to avoid them.

text.content: 1. Not Handling Environment Variables Securely

rich_text.plain_text: 1. Not Handling Environment Variables Securely

text.content: Environment variables are one of those things that seem simple until they bite you.

rich_text.plain_text: Environment variables are one of those things that seem simple until they bite you.

text.content: They’re useful for storing configuration values like API URLs, feature flags, and environment-specific settings. But in frontend apps, you have to be careful. Some environment variables are bundled into the JavaScript that gets sent to the browser. That means they are not private.

rich_text.plain_text: They’re useful for storing configuration values like API URLs, feature flags, and environment-specific settings. But in frontend apps, you have to be careful. Some environment variables are bundled into the JavaScript that gets sent to the browser. That means they are not private.

text.content: If a secret ends up in your client bundle, it is no longer a secret. Anyone can inspect the JavaScript and find it.

rich_text.plain_text: If a secret ends up in your client bundle, it is no longer a secret. Anyone can inspect the JavaScript and find it.

text.content: A good pattern is to keep sensitive values on the server and only expose values that are safe for the browser. You can also keep an example environment file in your repo so other developers know what values are needed:

text.content: The main rule is simple: if the browser needs it, assume users can see it. If it is sensitive, keep it server-side.

text.content: 2. Misconfiguring the Production Build

rich_text.plain_text: 2. Misconfiguring the Production Build

text.content: A common deployment mistake is assuming that if the app works locally, it is ready for production.

rich_text.plain_text: A common deployment mistake is assuming that if the app works locally, it is ready for production.

text.content: Development mode and production mode are not the same thing. Development builds are usually larger, slower, and include extra warnings or debugging behavior. Production builds are optimized for real users.

rich_text.plain_text: Development mode and production mode are not the same thing. Development builds are usually larger, slower, and include extra warnings or debugging behavior. Production builds are optimized for real users.

text.content: For most React apps, you want to run a proper production build before deploying:

text.content: It’s also worth testing the production build locally before shipping it. A surprising number of issues only show up after the app is built.

text.content: 3. Forgetting to Optimize Bundle Size

rich_text.plain_text: 3. Forgetting to Optimize Bundle Size

text.content: One of the fastest ways to make a React app feel slow is to ship too much JavaScript.

rich_text.plain_text: One of the fastest ways to make a React app feel slow is to ship too much JavaScript.

text.content: A big bundle means the browser has more code to download, parse, and execute before the user can really interact with the app. On a fast laptop, that might not seem like a big deal. On a mid-range phone with a weak connection, it can feel painfully slow. Minimize the bytes that are sent over the wire.

On a mid-range phone with a weak connection, it can feel painfully slow. Minimize the bytes that are sent over the wire.

text.content: 4. Skipping Error Monitoring and Logging

rich_text.plain_text: 4. Skipping Error Monitoring and Logging

text.content: Once your app is live, things will go wrong. That is not pessimism. That is just production.

rich_text.plain_text: Once your app is live, things will go wrong. That is not pessimism. That is just production.

text.content: Users will run into edge cases you did not test. APIs will fail. Browsers will behave differently. A deployment will look fine at first, then one route will quietly break for 15 percent of users.

text.content: 5. Ignoring Security Best Practices

rich_text.plain_text: 5. Ignoring Security Best Practices

text.content: Security can feel like something you deal with later, but production is exactly where small mistakes start to matter.

text.content: 6. Forgetting About Caching

rich_text.plain_text: 6. Forgetting About Caching

text.content: Caching can make your app much faster, but bad caching can create confusing production bugs.

rich_text.plain_text: Caching can make your app much faster, but bad caching can create confusing production bugs.

text.content: Static assets like JavaScript and CSS files are usually safe to cache for a long time when their filenames include a content hash. If the file changes, the filename changes too.

rich_text.plain_text: Static assets like JavaScript and CSS files are usually safe to cache for a long time when their filenames include a content hash. If the file changes, the filename changes too.

text.content: HTML and content pages are different. If those are cached too aggressively, users might load an old version of a page even after the content has been updated. This gets especially painful on publishing sites, where authors expect “publish” to mean “the page is live now.”

text.content: When something looks stale, it is not always obvious which layer is holding onto the old version. That can lead to the classic production debugging loop: the editor says the article is wrong, you refresh and see the new version, someone else still sees the old version, and now everyone is haunted.

text.content: This is where cache invalidation matters. For content-heavy apps, you usually want a reliable way to purge or revalidate specific pages when content changes. That might mean clearing CDN paths, using cache tags, calling a revalidation endpoint, or wiring your CMS publish event into your frontend cache strategy.

text.content: 7. Not Having a Rollback Plan

rich_text.plain_text: 7. Not Having a Rollback Plan

text.content: Every deployment should have an escape hatch.

rich_text.plain_text: Every deployment should have an escape hatch.

text.content: Even with good testing, things can break. A bad build can go out. A feature flag can behave unexpectedly. An API change can break a page you forgot about.
